title: Milk Adulterants and Their Detection
shortDescription: Common milk adulterants, why they are used and the simple and laboratory tests used to detect them.
genZNote: Milk adulteration tests are mini chemistry labs in a test tube. Starch → iodine, neutraliser → rosolic acid — match the sus ingredient to its test.

sections.heading: Adulterants and Tests
sections.body: FSSAI's DART and mobile "Food Safety on Wheels" labs support quick screening; legal action requires analysis by a notified laboratory.

table.caption: Milk adulteration guide
rows: Lactometer reading low; freezing point above −0.512 °C; lower SNF
Foam test; methylene blue/ bromocresol methods
Ferric chloride + conc. H2SO4 violet ring; Hehner test
Fatty acid profile; BR reading; chromatography

sections.heading: Lactometer and Fat Tests
bullets: Lactometer (Quevenne type) reads density; corrected lactometer reading (CLR) accounts for temperature; adulteration by water lowers it, skimming raises it.
Gerber method for fat: sulphuric acid + amyl alcohol, centrifuge, read butyrometer.
Milk analysers (ultrasonic, infrared) give fat/SNF/protein quickly; reference methods: Kjeldahl (protein), Rose–Gottlieb (fat).

sections.heading: Health Effects and Legal Position
bullets: Urea, detergents, formalin and hydrogen peroxide pose acute and chronic risks; melamine caused renal failure in infants.
Penalties follow FSS Act ss.51–59 depending on adulterant and harm; milk and milk products also fall under FSSAI standards.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Milk is adulterated to increase volume, solids or keeping quality; simple chemical tests and laboratory analysis detect adulterants.

commonTraps: Do not say home tests are legal proof.
